clinical_targets.goal: Complete alleviation of primary presenting complaint and systemic stability
Return of baseline physiological parameters (vital signs, CBC, metabolic panel)
Full return to activities of daily living (ADLs) and functional autonomy

steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Women's Health focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.role: Standard initial therapy for mild-to-moderate Women's Health.
drug_classes.dosing: Initiate standard therapeutic dosing; titrate over 2–4 weeks based on clinical response and tolerability.
drug_classes.pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Women's Health require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Women's Health.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Calculate CrCl using Cockcroft-Gault before prescribing narrow therapeutic index drugs.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Review patient's complete prescription and OTC medication list for drug-induced liver injury (DILI).
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Verify safety in pregnancy and lactation databases before prescribing any new therapeutic class.
special_populations.elderly: Perform medication reconciliation to eliminate unnecessary polypharmacy and anticholinergic load.

style_3_monograph.summary: Women have unique health issues. And some of the health issues that affect both men and women can affect women differently. Unique issues include pregnancy , menopause , and conditions of the female organs. Women can have a healthy pregnancy by getting early and regular prenatal care . They should also get recommended breast cancer, cervical cancer , and bone density screenings. Women and men also have many of the same health problems. But these problems can affect women differently. For example: Women are more likely to die following a heart attack than men Women are more likely to show signs of depression and anxiety than men The effects of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) can be more serious in women Osteoarthritis affects more women than men Women are more likely to have urinary tract problems NIH: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
style_3_monograph.treatment: Hirsutism is generally a long-term problem. There are many ways to remove or treat unwanted hair. Some treatment effects last longer than others. Medicines -- Medicines such as birth control pills, anti-androgen medicines, and spironolactone are a few options for some women. Electrolysis -- Electrical current is used to permanently damage individual hair follicles so they do not grow back. This method is expensive, and multiple treatments are needed. Swelling, scarring, and redness of the skin may occur. Laser energy directed at the dark color (melanin) in the hairs -- This method is best for a large area of very dark hair. It does not work on blond or red hair. Temporary options include: Shaving -- Although this does not cause more hair to grow, it may make hair look thicker. Chemicals, plucking, and waxing -- These options are safe and inexpensive. However, chemical products may irritate the skin. For women who are overweight, weight loss may be able to help reduce hair growth.
